name: Thanumalayan Temple, Suchindram
deity: The Trimurti as Sthanumalayan — Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma worshipped in a single lingam
period: Ancient origins; the great gateway, halls and musical pillars elaborated under the Nayaks
dynasty: Ancient origins; Chola, Vijayanagara and Nayaka elaboration
summary: Near the southern tip of India, Suchindram enshrines a rarity — the three great gods Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma worshipped together in a single lingam as Sthanumalayan — in a temple famous for its towering gateway, its musical stone pillars, and a giant image of Hanuman.

sections.history: The Thanumalayan temple at Suchindram, in the far south of Tamil Nadu near Nagercoil, is one of the region's great shrines. Its worship is ancient, and the temple as it stands was raised over long centuries — with Chola and Vijayanagara foundations and its most celebrated structures, the great gateway tower and the sculptured halls, elaborated under the Nayaks. Long administered from Travancore, the temple sits amid the paddy country of the deep south. Its very name reflects its unique character: Sthanu (Shiva), Mal (Vishnu) and Ayan (Brahma) united in one — Sthanumalayan.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered beneath a soaring white gateway tower, a landmark of the southern plain, and opens into a sequence of pillared halls worked in the mature Dravidian manner. Its most famous feature is the set of musical pillars, slender colonnettes carved from single blocks of stone that ring with musical notes when struck — among the most celebrated of their kind. The alankara mandapa carries some of the finest sculpture in the south, and a great image of Hanuman, carved from a single stone and standing some six metres tall, is a focus of devotion. At the heart of it all is the sanctum of the lingam worshipped as the three gods in one.
sections.legends: The name Suchindram is traditionally explained as the place where Indra, king of the gods, was purified — suchi meaning pure — of a curse, and by tradition Indra is said to worship here in the night. The temple's central mystery is its enshrinement of the Trimurti in one form: Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma, the powers of creation, preservation and dissolution, honoured together in a single lingam as Sthanumalayan, a rare theological vision made stone. Around this the temple gathers the legends of the south, of the goddess and of the gods who share the one sanctum.
sections.festivals: The temple's calendar is rich with festivals, chief among them the car festival, when the great temple car is drawn through Suchindram, and the Margazhi and Navaratri observances. Music has a special place here, fitting for the temple of the singing pillars, and festival nights fill the pillared halls with lamps and crowds. The teppam, or float festival, is held on the temple tank.
sections.experience: Suchindram rewards the unhurried visitor: the ring of the musical pillars, the sculpture of the halls, the towering white gopuram and the giant Hanuman give the temple a character all its own, and its unique Trimurti sanctum sets it apart among the shrines of the south. It lies a short journey from Nagercoil and from Kanyakumari at the land's end, with which it is naturally joined into a pilgrimage of the deep south.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a long midday closure; festival days are busiest. Confirm current timings before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Men are traditionally asked to remove the upper garment before entering the sanctum, as at many southern shrines; follow the posted rules.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted, especially in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Suchindram is in Kanyakumari district at the southern end of Tamil Nadu, about 7 km from Nagercoil and a short journey from Kanyakumari, well connected by road.
